content.title: Infinite Limits and Asymptotes
content.overview: This lesson focuses on the behavior of functions as they approach specific values or as the input grows without bound. We define vertical asymptotes through infinite limits and horizontal asymptotes through limits at infinity, providing the foundation for understanding unbounded function behavior.
learning_objectives: Define and identify vertical asymptotes using one-sided infinite limits.
Determine horizontal asymptotes by evaluating limits as x approaches positive or negative infinity.
Apply algebraic techniques to determine the end behavior of rational and transcendental functions.
Justify the existence of asymptotes using proper limit notation.

sections.title: Vertical Asymptotes and Infinite Limits
sections.content: A vertical asymptote occurs at x = c if the function f(x) increases or decreases without bound as x approaches c from either the left or the right. Formally, if the limit of f(x) as x approaches c (from the left, right, or both) is infinity or negative infinity, then the line x = c is a vertical asymptote. In rational functions, this typically occurs at values of x that make the denominator zero while the numerator remains non-zero.

sections.title: Horizontal Asymptotes and Limits at Infinity
sections.content: Horizontal asymptotes describe the end behavior of a function. The line y = L is a horizontal asymptote if the limit of f(x) as x approaches infinity (or negative infinity) equals L. For rational functions, compare the degrees of the numerator (n) and denominator (d): if n < d, the asymptote is y = 0; if n = d, the asymptote is the ratio of the leading coefficients; if n > d, there is no horizontal asymptote (though there may be a slant asymptote).

sections.title: Justification and Notation
sections.content:
On the AP Exam, simply stating a value is insufficient for justification. To justify a vertical asymptote at x = c, you must show that the limit as x approaches c from at least one side is infinite. To justify a horizontal asymptote at y = L, you must evaluate the limit as x approaches infinity and show it equals L. Note that a function can cross a horizontal asymptote, but it cannot cross a vertical asymptote where it is undefined.

![A sequence of steps to identify asymptotes: Factor and simplify, find zeros of denominator for vertical asymptotes, compare degrees for horizontal asymptotes, and write formal limit justifications.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/ce402918-6869-43e1-ba74-1ba1b937fc37-1786526286932-452.webp)

worked_examples.question: Let f(x) = (2x^2 - 8) / (x^2 - 5x + 6). Identify all vertical and horizontal asymptotes and justify your answers using limits.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Factor the function. f(x) = [2(x-2)(x+2)] / [(x-2)(x-3)]. Step 2: Simplify. f(x) = 2(x+2) / (x-3) for x ≠ 2. Step 3: Vertical Asymptotes. The denominator is zero at x=3. As x approaches 3 from the right, f(x) approaches infinity. Thus, x=3 is a vertical asymptote. (Note: x=2 is a removable discontinuity, not an asymptote). Step 4: Horizontal Asymptotes. Evaluate the limit as x approaches infinity. Since the degrees are equal (2), the limit is the ratio of leading coefficients: 2/1 = 2. Thus, y=2 is the horizontal asymptote.

common_mistakes: Assuming every zero of the denominator is a vertical asymptote; it must not be canceled by a zero in the numerator.
Forgetting to check both positive and negative infinity for horizontal asymptotes, especially in functions involving square roots or exponentials.
Confusing the equations: vertical asymptotes are 'x =', horizontal asymptotes are 'y ='.
exam_tips: Always simplify the expression first to identify 'holes' (removable discontinuities) versus vertical asymptotes.
When evaluating limits at infinity for rational functions, divide every term by the highest power of x in the denominator.
Use the notation 'f(x) -> infinity' or 'limit = infinity' to describe unbounded growth.
content.recap: Infinite limits describe the behavior of a function near vertical asymptotes (x = c), while limits at infinity describe the end behavior or horizontal asymptotes (y = L). Mastery of these concepts requires both algebraic manipulation and formal limit notation for justification.

knowledge_claims.content: A vertical asymptote exists at x = c if the limit of f(x) as x approaches c from the left or right is positive or negative infinity.
A horizontal asymptote exists at y = L if the limit of f(x) as x approaches positive or negative infinity is equal to L.
For a rational function where the degree of the numerator is less than the degree of the denominator, the horizontal asymptote is y = 0.
For a rational function where the degrees of the numerator and denominator are equal, the horizontal asymptote is the ratio of the leading coefficients.
A zero in the denominator does not guarantee a vertical asymptote if that same factor also appears in the numerator and cancels out, creating a removable discontinuity.
Infinite limits represent unbounded behavior where the function values grow or shrink without limit as the input approaches a specific value.
Unlike vertical asymptotes, which a function cannot cross at the point of discontinuity, a function's graph may cross its horizontal asymptote multiple times.
To justify a horizontal asymptote on the AP exam, one must explicitly write and evaluate the limit of the function as x approaches infinity or negative infinity.
In the function f(x) = e^x, a horizontal asymptote exists at y = 0 as x approaches negative infinity, but no horizontal asymptote exists as x approaches positive infinity.
If the limit of f(x) as x approaches c from the left is infinity and from the right is negative infinity, x = c is still considered a vertical asymptote.
When evaluating limits at infinity for functions with square roots, such as sqrt(x^2), remember that sqrt(x^2) = |x|, which affects the sign of the limit as x approaches negative infinity.
To verify a vertical asymptote at x = c, check if the simplified form of the function has a denominator that equals zero at c while the numerator is non-zero.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Infinite Limits and Asymptotes — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Infinite Limits and Asymptotes: Unbounded function behavior near an input can identify a vertical asymptote, while end behavior can identify horizontal or slant tendencies.
options.B: Derivatives of Inverse Functions: The derivative of an inverse at an output is the reciprocal of the original derivative at the corresponding input when that derivative is nonzero.
options.C: Increasing, Decreasing, and Critical Points: The sign of the first derivative determines intervals of increase and decrease and helps classify local extrema at critical points.
options.D: Integration by Parts and Partial Fractions: Integration by parts reverses the product rule, while partial fractions decomposes rational functions into simpler integrable terms.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because Unbounded function behavior near an input can identify a vertical asymptote, while end behavior can identify horizontal or slant tendencies. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Infinite Limits and Asymptotes — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Exponential, Logarithmic, and Inverse Trigonometric Derivatives: Standard derivatives for exponential, logarithmic, and inverse trigonometric functions combine with product, quotient, and chain rules.
options.B: Infinite Limits and Asymptotes: Unbounded function behavior near an input can identify a vertical asymptote, while end behavior can identify horizontal or slant tendencies.
options.C: Concavity and Inflection Points: The sign of the second derivative determines concavity, and an inflection point requires an actual change in concavity.
options.D: Improper Integrals: An improper integral is defined by a limit at an infinite bound or unbounded integrand and converges only when that limit is finite.

items.explanation: Choice B is best because Unbounded function behavior near an input can identify a vertical asymptote, while end behavior can identify horizontal or slant tendencies. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.
